presentingComplaint: Transient loss of consciousness while climbing stairs
history: 74-year-old man with an 8-month history of progressive exertional breathlessness and chest tightness that resolves with rest. Today he had a witnessed syncopal episode while walking up a flight of stairs, with rapid spontaneous recovery and no post-ictal confusion or incontinence. Two prior near-syncope episodes on exertion over the past month. Background of long-standing hypertension. No palpitations preceding the event, no focal neurology, no tongue-biting. Non-smoker, no diabetes.
examination: Alert, GCS 15. Slow-rising, low-volume (parvus et tardus) carotid pulse. Ejection systolic murmur, loudest at the right upper sternal edge, radiating to both carotids, with a soft/absent A2 and a sustained (heaving) apex beat. No signs of pulmonary oedema at rest, no raised JVP, chest clear. No focal neurological deficit, no meningism, no calf swelling.
imaging: Transthoracic echocardiography: severe calcific aortic stenosis — aortic valve area 0.8 cm2, peak velocity 4.4 m/s, mean gradient 52 mmHg, with concentric LV hypertrophy and preserved ejection fraction. ECG: sinus rhythm with LV hypertrophy and strain pattern, no acute ischaemia. Chest X-ray: normal heart size, no pulmonary oedema.
differentialDiagnoses: Severe aortic stenosis with exertional syncope
Arrhythmic syncope (e.g. paroxysmal AV block / VT)
finalDiagnosis: Severe symptomatic calcific aortic stenosis presenting with exertional syncope
citations: ACC/AHA Management of Valvular Heart Disease 2020
contraindications: Avoid vasodilators / GTN and other preload-reducing agents in severe AS (risk of profound hypotension)
Caution with beta-blockers or negative inotropes given fixed obstruction
Avoid aggressive diuresis — these patients are preload-dependent
edgeCases: Low-flow low-gradient severe AS with reduced EF or paradoxical low-flow with preserved EF may under-estimate severity on gradient alone — requires dobutamine stress echo / valve calcium scoring
Exertional syncope in AS is an ominous symptom (untreated survival ~2-3 years) and mandates expedited valve-intervention referral
expectedMaiK: Exertional syncope with a slow-rising pulse and an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids in an elderly patient strongly suggests severe symptomatic aortic stenosis. This is a class I indication for aortic valve replacement (SAVR/TAVI); avoid preload-reducing drugs and arrange urgent echocardiography and heart-team referral.
expectedNextQuestions: Was the syncope clearly exertional, and is there associated exertional angina or breathlessness?
Any features suggesting arrhythmia (palpitations, family history of sudden death) as an alternative cause?
expectedInvestigations: Transthoracic echocardiogram to quantify valve area and gradient
12-lead ECG and telemetry/ambulatory monitoring to exclude arrhythmic syncope
Coronary assessment prior to valve intervention
